posts.author: Archeia
posts.body:
Heavily inspired by Japanese dev forums!
Please share your silly mistakes or embarrassing stories that happened while making games, releasing them… and so on. If they end up being funny stories
and
good lessons, that’d be ideal… I guess?
Example Blooper from M-san:
"The game I released had a game-breaking bug right at the beginning, but no one reported it."
…Well, it
was
quietly released on a personal site under my main alias, where traffic is limited, so I suppose it’s not surprising no one said anything.
Still, it was both embarrassing and just plain sad…
The one who told me about it was a friend who had recently returned to their debugging role.
Due to certain circumstances, they had taken a break from debugging for a while, so this was about a game I released during the time I was developing alone.
It happened because I overlooked the issue—so it’s 100% my fault.
It was an incident that reminded me just how crucial debugging really is.
…Which basically means, uh, no one was playing it anyway—
ahem
.
Click to expand...
"I focused too much on aesthetics and gameplay, and ended up with a structurally absurd building"
"This wall looks so empty... okay, let’s add a window!"
→ Upon thinking it over, I realized you
shouldn’t
be able to see outside from there (and it’d actually be weird if you could).
"Let’s add a supply room here!"
"Oops, I forgot to make a room needed for a later part of the game… guess I’ll just stick it here!"
"This dungeon feels too short… time to expand!"
→ And thus, I ended up creating a building that would leave even professional architects dumbfounded. ＼(^o^)／
I only noticed the mess
after release
, which was incredibly embarrassing.
Since then, I’ve made a habit of being more mindful of building structures when designing houses or architecture-based dungeons. Especially for large buildings like castles, I now draw
floor plans on paper
before jumping into development.
Click to expand...
"Lost data due to OS issues on my old PC, and accidentally deleted needed assets on my current one"
Old PC Incident (Ubuntu)
Back when I was using Ubuntu on my old PC, I couldn't use RPG Maker, so I was just working on assets ahead of time.
Then the OS ran into issues and I couldn’t recover it on my own, so I reinstalled it.
Later on, I realized that
some original image files—like logos and character illustrations—were gone
and no longer editable.
My reaction:
"Welp, I screwed up… welp."
I had thought,
“Well, I’ve backed up the exported versions of all my data, so even if something gets deleted, it’s no big deal. Time to reinstall the OS!”
But yeah… turns out there actually
was
important stuff I didn’t back up.
Current PC Incident
To free up space on my current PC, I decided to do a clean sweep of my “Downloads” folder.
I thought,
“All the assets I downloaded should already be inside the project folder anyway, so it’s fine.”
But of course—I’d
forgotten to move a few things
, so I had to re-download them.
To make matters worse, I also deleted
some free software I had installed to support game development
.
Asset management really is important, huh.
Click to expand...
From KANNAZUKI SASUKE
"We divided map and event creation between two people, but our variables collided"
This happened when we were working on a sample game for
RPG Maker MZ
. The two of us split up the work of creating maps and events. We created maps with different IDs in separate projects and merged them as they were completed.
However, my collaborator placed their variables immediately after mine, which were named something like "XX1", without checking. As a result, the variables we used overlapped perfectly.
Normally, you'd assume that if someone is using a variable like "XX1", the other person would continue with "XX2", "XX3", and so on—so at the very least, you’d leave a buffer of 10 or so IDs. But my partner didn’t do that. When I pointed it out and complained, they did admit it was careless on their part.
It really showed that when working collaboratively, you must
establish a proper system for shared variables and switches
ahead of time.
Click to expand...
"The English help text for an official MV plugin was shown to a translation company—and they practically rewrote it"
I created an official plugin for
RPG Maker MV
, which included help documentation in both Japanese and English.
The editorial team submitted it to a translation agency to have the English reviewed.
However, they apparently sent over my awkward English text
as-is
to the translators.
The returned Excel file was filled with notes like “The English was slightly unnatural, so we revised it” on nearly every line.
Even small grammar issues, like using “each items” instead of the correct “each item,” were flagged and corrected.
I ended up just
exposing my clumsy English skills
.
Back in school, I scored only
520 on the TOEIC
, while most of my peers had over 600. Please cut me some slack.
But really, if they were going to get it properly translated anyway,
why did they have to include my shaky English draft at all?
It was unbelievably embarrassing—like I wanted to crawl into a hole and disappear.
Click to expand...
"A plugin included in the MZ launch lineup caused an error on execution and went unfixed for over half a year"
One of the launch plugins, called
ChangeSelectItemWindowMZ.js
, was designed to customize the size, position, number of rows, and columns in the "Select Item" window.
However, in its initial version, it called a function that existed in MV but not in MZ, which caused an error.
Shockingly,
no one discovered this until about six months after MZ was released
.
It was later fixed, but the fact that it went unnoticed for so long means… well, no one was using the plugin, I guess.
Click to expand...
"I created a dungeon puzzle that not a single test player from the editorial team could solve"
In the RPG Maker MZ sample game, there was a puzzle based on
the three primary colors of light and pigment
.
You couldn’t progress without solving it—but then I received a report saying:
"None of the test players were able to solve it."
In a rush, I added a character who gives hints in three stages, which saved the day.
But I realized:
extremely difficult puzzles should be optional
, like unlocking a room with a treasure chest—
not mandatory for story progression. Lesson learned.
Click to expand...
"An event froze if you talked to a character from the side, due to a 'Set Movement Route' configuration"
This one’s from an RPG Maker MV sample.
There was a person standing in front of a library. If you chose “I want to go ahead,” they would step aside to the left.
However, if you talked to them from the left side, their movement couldn't complete—
and the game froze
.
I fixed it immediately in the next version, but still…
I couldn't help thinking, “What a dumb mistake to make.”
Click to expand...
From UFO_1122
"I implemented random treasure chests, and... the drop rates taught me a lesson"
In my current project, I'm working on implementing
randomized treasure chests
.
Naturally, rarer items are supposed to appear
less frequently
than common ones.
At first, I thought:
“Huh, why do these low-probability rare items keep showing up more than the common ones?”
↓
“After several playthroughs, it balanced out and the drop rates flipped as expected. So it was just a streak, huh.”
↓
“Wait… I just checked the settings and realized—my rarity values were reversed… huh??”
Click to expand...
…Yep. That happened.
People often talk about the
“law of large numbers”
or
probability convergence
, but this experience reminded me: in a sample size small enough for a human to realistically test,
outcomes can skew wildly
, and it's totally normal.
It was a humbling reminder that
both probability bias and incorrect settings can look deceptively similar
at first glance.
Click to expand...

posts.author: Cythera
posts.body:
Ah-hahaha...my top favs (and, if I'm being honest, there's a
lot
more than these) include:
Playtesting a cutscene, tweaking the smallest thing and thinking 'there's no way this impacts the rest of the scene! It's fine!'. Deploy, upload, and...the cutscene ran with the characters invisible
A jam game I made a while ago had a 6-char party. Because, it was a game about death. I fully expected players to lose a char or two. It was impossible to lose because the MC was effectively immortal. Well, there was a cutscene that ran differently depending on who was still alive in the party with the MC. Never considered the possibility a player might kill all 5 side chars before that cutscene, and never made a branch for that...so the cutscene never ran. Thankfully, someone caught it and told me about it before the deadline haha!
Optional boss battle kept breaking for one of my testers in my main project; could not figure out why the game softlocked and the boss couldn't be targeted? That's such a bizarre bug! Turns out, it was the way I handle the perma-kill passive of the MC in my game! The softlock required multiple conditions in a strict order, so it wasn't a very likely event, hence why it took so long to pin down. I actually curled up on the floor laughing when I finally figured it out. The fix? Make the boss resist a specific placeholder state for the perma-kill passive ._. 10 seconds. Done.
Not a blooper, because it's a fully intended mechanic, but something I will always find hilarious is when I was playtesting my game. MC has a critical rate buff on himself. Gets confused by an enemy, hits himself, crits, kills himself, and because of his perma-kill passive, can't be revived till after the fight!

Alright, fine.. I'll fess up.
I had created a boss battle wherein when the boss was healed so were all his adds, and when the boss was defeated, so were all his adds via a Linked Health/Linked Defeat set up.
When I went to play test tackling the boss using the intended strat, it worked perfectly.

posts.author: TG22
posts.body:
OK guys, prepare the rotten tomatoes, you will need them.
First, my game is released monthly, each update adding a few quests or bits of the main story. So yes, we are talking about a released thing, not a mistake that never left the coder's computer!
About one year ago I had an idea on how to improve the main character, but I needed to add him a new starting skill (level 1 skill). To do so the solution was to perform what I call a "character reset" when loading an old save.
So I wrote a plugin that could save everything (except the skills) about a character (current XP, equipped items, current HP/MP/TP, paramPlus, states, position in party) to restore it later. So all I had to do was save the character data using my plugin, remove him from the party and adding him back with the initialize option on. Then restore the saved status.
Which was working perfecly... except that I forgot to save the character's name, that you can enter when creating a new game. So for a few weeks every player had their main character with his default name, "Ralph" !
As the data was completely lost, all I could do the next month was to offer a character rename.
Now I'm no longer testing the game using the default name!

posts.author: Banana_Duck
posts.body:
Reviving this topic because I have another blooper to share.
I was making a cutscene that includes the increase of a variable's value. To make sure I don't use the wrong variable, I named this one "Story".
I used the variable as a switch, so after a map transfer, my cutscene keeps going through a different autorun event.
I tried testing and... no luck. The first autorun event proceeded like planned, but the second event didn't trigger at all. What did I do wrong? Was it another event on this second map? Did one of my hundred scripts mess up with my messages somehow?
As it turns out, my second event was triggered by a different variable, one that isn't the "Story" one, but instead the database's first variable, which is one as a placeholder.
So yeah, check your variables and switches.

posts.author: AphoticAmaranth
posts.body:
My game, Dream Magic Heroes, had quite a few bugs and issues that somehow went unnoticed until about a year after the full release, which I only discovered during the development of post-game/hard mode. Oopsie.
Guess that means not enough people play my games huh
A couple of notable ones:
I have an Incurable status, which reduces healing received to 0. I also have a character with the Sweet Tooth passive, which increases healing received from sweet food. This was mostly done by having certain heals/items be classified as "Sweet" element, while Sweet Tooth increased the element rate of the Sweet element.
However, I also was using a plugin to change the damage popup numbers, which by default included popups for elemental weaknesses. Normally, this only applied to effects that deal 0 or more damage, and does not affect heals, since healing is basically negative damage. But if you had both Incurable and Sweet Tooth, and attempted to heal using a sweet item/ability, then Incurable would reduce the healing to 0, which then makes it eligible for elemental weakness popups, and I did use elemental weaknesses for Sweet Tooth...
Similarly, I had passives and equipment with effects that triggered when you evade an attack. However, I also had a couple of statuses, Paranoia and Distrust, which cause you to evade your allies' support abilities... and also triggered those evasion effects.
After testing and confirming that Incurable and Paranoia work as intended, I'd assume there's no reason to even try healing/supporting an affected ally, unless you're using a multi-target ability
or fail the reading comprehension check.
However, during the development of post-game, I introduced Distrust, which unlike Paranoia, does not expire but instead has stacks that only go down when evading a support ability. It was only while testing a variety of different party compositions against the one boss that applied Distrust that I realised this issue.
I guess the main takeaway from all this is,
test everything, including things that you wouldn't expect any rational person to do.
And
test every aspect of plugins, including features you don't use or need.
There was also a bit of a balance issue with Paralyze, which has a chance to cause affected targets to skip their next action. In all the testing I've done, over the course of long boss battles, it tends to even out and felt balanced, especially since bosses tend to have higher Constitution (which mitigates the chance of Paralyze procs). But of course, there would be a couple of exceptions...
There's a gimmick battle against an enemy that applied Guilt to everyone, which instantly kills if it reaches 10 stacks. Guilt stacks can be transferred to others by attacking or supporting, and the enemy in question had too much HP/DEF/RES to realistically be killed by attacking it until it reached 0 HP, so the intended solution was to have everyone stack Guilt on them. This should only take a few turns at most, and if you failed to do so, you'd get wiped... or so I thought. But one player managed to avoid letting Guilt stacks ever get too high via Paralyze/Sleep spam, thus making the battle drag on way longer than it needed to. I've since nerfed the stats to make winning via damage more doable, and also made an achievement for doing so.
Then there was that one time I made a post-game boss, and during testing, accidentally trivialised it with a (un)lucky streak of Paralyze procs.
In the end, I decided to implement pseudo-RNG for Paralyze procs, which should hopefully prevent such (un)lucky streaks.
Unrelated to RPG Maker, but this one time I made a game with an in-game date/time system. Except at the end of the month I changed the day but forgot to change the month, so someone thought there was time travel or something.
